## Как это читать

121 находка — это 121 *вердикт*, и почти каждый вердикт сработал на двух-трёх основаниях сразу. Ниже — вид ошибки, а не строка отчёта; поэтому суммы по видам больше 121. Порядок — по цене: сколько находок каждый вид съел.

## 1. Следствие ложно, потому что механизм живёт этажом выше или ниже — 31 находка

Самый дорогой вид и он же самый уже описанный. Идентификатор действительно не подключён; ошибка в том, что находка приписывает этому **последствие**, которое кто-то другой уже закрывает.

- `agent-sdk/subagents` — «Agent-вызов без `run_in_background` уходит в фон на любой глубине»: `spawner.ts:540` правда содержит `args.background ?? (depth === 1)`, но `spawner.ts:518` отказывает при `depth > maxDepth` (`DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH = 1`) — до строки 540 вложенный вызов не доходит вообще.
- `agent-sdk/subagents` — «`effort` числом молча отбрасывается»: доказательства ссылаются на `definitions.ts:403` и `:453` и перескакивают одиннадцать строк между ними, где `:424-425` бросает `Invalid ${label}.effort`. Отказ громкий и по имени.
- `changelog` / `whats-new/2026-w29` — «нет пер-сессионного потолка спавнов»: находка остановилась ровно на одну строку раньше нужной. `spawner.ts:603` — `fanout: cfg.maxFanout ?? 100`, и `child-session-service.ts:148` бросает `child-session-fanout-limit` по полному append-only списку детей.
- `permissions` — цитируемая как доказательство `isWholeCapabilityDeniedByPermissionDsl` (`permission-dsl.ts:900-905`) имеет **ноль продакшн-вызовов**; заявленный вред невозможен через мёртвую функцию.

**Проверка:** следствие проверяется отдельно от идентификатора и **в обе стороны от места находки** — на вызывающего и на вызываемого. Правило: прежде чем писать «поэтому X происходит/не происходит», найти и прочитать все продакшн-callers цитируемого символа (ноль callers — уже отказ) и его вызываемых на один уровень; и предъявить исполненный положительный контроль, что X действительно не происходит.

## 2. Не та подсистема: однофамилец или однопризванец в соседнем модуле — 19 находок

- `skills` — бюджет листинга скиллов замерен по `pi-harness/capability-catalog.ts`, у которого kinds — `'builtin' | 'session' | 'plugin' | 'mcp' | 'app'`, и **никакого skill-kind там нет**: это каталог инструментов харнеса, а не листинг скиллов.
- `corporate-launcher` — «SHELL_PREFIX не обёртывает Bash/hooks/stdio-MCP»: якорь `SessionManager.ts:16320` лежит внутри `executeDirectShellCommand`, чей единственный продакшн-вызов — bang-режим композера. Ни одного из трёх названных страницей путей.
- `troubleshooting` — `USE_BUILTIN_RIPGREP=0`: страница сама ограничивает область в открывающей строке секции (`Search tool, @file mentions, custom agents, custom skills`), а `resolveRipgrepPath` в находке кормит `searchSessions` — полнотекстовый поиск по истории сессий, которого у Claude Code нет вовсе.
- `whats-new/2026-w28` — «auto mode должен блокировать правки транскрипта» уперлось в `removal-circuit-breaker.ts`, который реализует root/home-порог из `permissions.md` и срабатывает во **всех** режимах, включая bypass. Другой механизм, другая страница.

**Проверка:** назвать подсистему в самой формулировке находки («для subagents, не для skills»; «для оболочки Electron, не для CLI-клиента»). И перед фиксацией — прочитать открывающую строку секции документации: она почти всегда содержит область действия, которую отдельная процитированная строка уже не несёт.

**Проверка:** до подачи — `rg -a` по имени ключа не только в исходниках, а и в `docs/superpowers/plans/`, `2026-07-29-inert-worklist.md` §3 и в реестре девиаций; и сравнить **даты**: дату страницы (`Week NN`, feature pill `vX.Y.Z`) с датой плана, а не только их существование.

**Проверка:** команду из находки прогнать заново, целиком, в том же shell, и вклеить её реальный вывод — не пересказ. Обязательно `grep -a` (в дереве есть файлы с NUL-байтом). **Проверка:** каждый якорь читается заново в момент подачи, и в находку выносится **процитированная строка исходника**, а не только номер. Имя символа проверяется существованием: `rg -a '\b<name>\b'` — ноль попаданий означает, что якорь придуман. Номера, унаследованные из прежних планов, считаются просроченными по умолчанию.

## 7. НОВОЕ. Отсутствие ручки прочитано как отсутствие поведения — 9 находок

**Проверка:** до подачи разложить претензию на «нет ключа» и «нет поведения» и доказывать вторую отдельно — исполнением, а не грепом. Спросить, не является ли наш вариант безусловным или более строгим: тогда это соответствие, а не расхождение.

## 12. Сфабрикованная цитата — 3 находки

Мало по числу, но это единственный вид, который убивает находку в один шаг.

- `permissions` — `Skill(<name pattern>)` подан как строка таблицы со страницы, где слово `skill` встречается дважды и ни разу как правило. Настоящий контракт — `skills.md:603-627`.
- `mcp-quickstart` — «`✘ Rejected (see disabledMcpjsonServers in settings)`»: на странице `Rejected` — 0 вхождений, `disabledMcpjsonServers` — 0. Придуманы и строка таблицы, и привязка к настройке, и даже команда (таблица статусов принадлежит `claude mcp list`, не `claude mcp get`).
- `agent-sdk/session-storage` — слово `timeout` не встречается в 306 строках страницы ни разу; предложение живёт на `agent-sdk/python.md:868`, с twin'ом на `typescript.md:431`, помеченным `*Alpha.*`.

**Проверка:** цитата подтверждается подстрочным сравнением в скрипте (`substring` в Python), а не глазом, и в находку идут md5 и число строк скачанной страницы. Слаг страницы в находке должен быть тем, откуда взята цитата: если контракт лежит на другой странице, находка переезжает туда, а не «self-discloses».

## 13. НОВОЕ. Вред заявлен на пути, недостижимом ни в одной сборке — 3 находки

**Проверка:** для каждой находки предъявить путь от поставляемого артефакта до заявленного вреда — какой флаг, какой билд, какое действие пользователя. Литеральный `false` без env-override и функция без callers — это доказательство недостижимости, и вред тогда не существует.

`hook-event-roster` ведёт всю hooks-половину. Она расширяет `AGENT_EVENT_CONTRACTS_V1` — версионированный инвентарь, который одновременно является словарём принимаемых значений для `automations.json` и зеркалится в предсобранный Pi-бандл. Отсюда следует правило релизного порядка (конфиг с новым именем события падает на старой сборке; host и subprocess едут из одной сборки), и это правило обязаны соблюдать три остальных hooks-плана. Дальше hooks идут строго цепочкой, потому что все они правят `automations/types.ts` и `lifecycle-bridge.ts`, а `git commit <pathspec>` берёт состояние рабочего дерева: `hook-input-payload-parity` → `hook-output-and-process-env`, и отдельно `hook-firing-and-await` — позже всех, о нём ниже.

**Затем настроечная волна**, от общего к частному: `managed-policy-sources` (каналы и правило «источники не сливаются»), `sandbox-path-settings`, `model-selection-defaults`, `statusline-surfaces`. Все четыре — persistence и delivered-policy, то есть risk trigger; ни одна не может быть написана до того, как словарь ключей зафиксирован.

**Память** идёт своей цепочкой, и её первый шаг обязателен: `memory-load-limits` переносит лимит в 200 строк на маршрут, которым читается каждый ход, и вводит отсутствующие 25KB. Пока этого нет, `memory-import-recognition` и `memory-write-feedback` меняли бы то, что не измеряется. Замыкает `memory-discovery-scopes` — она правит тот же `native-sources.ts`.

**MCP** — `mcp-server-config-and-connect` первым, потому что он определяет, что вообще может сказать конфиг сервера и с каким env/headers мы подключаемся; на нём стоят `mcp-roots-and-channels` (тот же `client.ts`) и `tool-result-size-thresholds`.

**Headless CLI** идёт после MCP по содержательной причине: `headless-init-frame` обязан заполнить `mcp_server_errors`, а какие конфиги считаются ошибочными, решает предыдущая единица. За ним `headless-cli-flags-and-exit` — тот же `apps/cli/src/index.ts`, и байтовый cap должен считать уже существующий init-кадр.

**Здесь становится понятен единственный неочевидный порядок:** `hook-firing-and-await` идёт после headless, а не рядом с остальными hooks. Ему нужен launch mode (`--init-only`, `-p --init`, `-p --maintenance`), которого в продукте нет, то есть новый флаг в том же файле CLI и новое поле в session-create RPC. Дешевле добавить флаг к уже зафиксированному контракту флагов, чем наоборот. Это же самая опасная единица набора: она меняет смысл уже сохранённых записей `automations.json` без изменения схемы — сохранённый catch-all `Setup` перестаёт срабатывать каждую сессию.

**Оркестрация** имеет свой локальный ведущий: `subagent-nesting-depth` (глубина 1 против документированных 3) обязан лечь первым, потому что фикстуры и арифметика семафоров всех следующих планов написаны под текущую глубину. Далее `subagent-limits-and-child-output`, `agent-memory-directories` (ждёт ещё и memory-планов — общий `memory-store.ts`), `agent-definition-fields`, `workflow-invocation-contract`.

**Skills и команды** — `skill-visibility-settings` первой: в ней оседает семантика `disable-model-invocation`/`user-invocable`, которую потом потребляют `skill-frontmatter-runtime`, `skill-discovery-precedence`, `custom-command-expansion` и `code-review-contract`. Рядом, независимо, `builtin-session-commands` (`/clear`, `/btw`, `/recap` — один парсер и один wire-union) и `shell-command-response-mode`.

**Worktrees и расписания** — `worktree-lifecycle` перед `scheduled-task-catchup` (запуску по расписанию нужен worktree); `loop-and-self-paced-scheduling` независима, это другой планировщик (`shared/sessions/cron-*`, а не `shared/automations/*`).

**Плагины** — `marketplace-auto-update` → `plugin-install-and-dependencies` → `plugin-bundle-component-shapes` (последняя ждёт ещё и `statusline-surfaces`: плагинный `subagentStatusLine` некуда направить, пока механизма нет).

**Независимые, и одну из них стоит взять раньше формального места в списке.** `egress-and-provider-routing` содержит утечку: 30x от гейтвея сегодня пересылает JWT на третий хост, потому что на двух fetch-вызовах нет `redirect: 'error'`. Формально она ни от чего не зависит и может ехать в любой волне — но это единственная строка набора, где цена ожидания измеряется в утёкшем секрете. Тем же свойством обладают `deep-link-safety` (ссылка извне процесса дёргает state-mutating RPC без действия пользователя) и `project-trust-home-carveout` ($HOME получает постоянный grant).

Остальные независимые — `permission-tool-classification`, `output-styles`, `claude-informational-messages`, `keybindings-config`, `goal-completion-state`, `web-search-budget`, `host-diagnostics-rpc` — можно ставить куда угодно, при одном ограничении: многие из них трогают `apps/cli/src/index.ts` или `packages/shared/src/capabilities/native-sources.ts`, и по правилу зонирования по файлам две такие единицы не идут параллельно.

units.name: managed-settings-key-vocabulary
units.title: Documented settings keys our strict parser strips, rejects, or enforces under another name
units.why: All five are the same defect at the same gate: `refuseUnknownKeys` (managed-policy.ts:727-733) and `StoredConfigTopLevelSchema` (validators.ts:208) drop or reject a documented Claude key, so a working Claude Code settings block reads as deployed and enforces nothing. `strictPluginOnlyCustomization` (f017/f110) has three of its four quarters already implemented under Nessy names such as `allowManagedHooksOnly`; `env` (f163) is worse than absent because strict parse fails the whole file closed; instruction-excludes (f185) is implemented at one scope out of four and the managed schema rejects the key; the auto-mode allowlist (f121) has correct sentinel and splice logic and no operand. One plan must fix the alias-vs-new-key policy and the strict-parse failure mode once, because every settings-shaped unit downstream copies that decision.
units.rationale: An administrator can paste a working Claude Code managed-settings block and have it actually lock what it says, and a user can write the documented `env` block without breaking config loading. Crosses a persistence boundary (the on-disk shape of `config.json`, `.claude/settings*.json` and the admin-authored managed policy) and a wire boundary (`ManagedPiPolicyV1` also arrives host-delivered), so key widening must be forward-compatible in both directions and the plan needs the strict-report and delivered-policy suites on the final diff.

units.name: hook-event-roster
units.title: Widen the documented hook-event roster and fix documented-but-unemitted classification
units.why: Three of the four are the same missing event, `DirectoryAdded`, filed off three different pages, and the fourth, `MessageDisplay`, is missing in exactly the same shape. Both fail the adapter's own written rule at `format-adapters.ts:634-635` - a documented-but-unemitted event is a deferral, not an unknown name - only because neither name ever reached `DEFERRED_EXTERNAL_HOOK_EVENT_REASONS`. The bound file set is one: `PluginHookEventName`, `PLUGIN_HOOK_EVENTS`, `AGENT_EVENT_CONTRACTS_V1`, `CLAUDE_HOOK_EVENT_MAP`, `PLUGIN_HOOK_EVENT_TO_AGENT_EVENT`, plus the stale 30-documented-events counts at `hooks-runtime.ts:13` and `format-adapters.ts:118`. It leads the hooks family because every other hooks plan edits those same tables.
units.rationale: A Claude plugin whose `hooks/hooks.json` declares `DirectoryAdded` or `MessageDisplay` imports with a routed deferral reason instead of a typo-shaped warning, and the two events become nameable in a hooks config. Crosses a persistence boundary - `AGENT_EVENTS` is the accepted-vocabulary zod enum for `automations.json` and for user/project hooks-config files - and a versioned inventory mirrored into the prebuilt Pi bundle (`apps/electron/resources/pi-agent-server/index.js`), so host and subprocess must ship from one build and a config written with a new name errors on an older build. That release-ordering rule is the plan's first section.

units.name: managed-policy-sources
units.title: The missing managed-policy source channels and the policyHelper executable
units.why: f027 and f109 are the same absent mechanism (`policyHelper`: unrecognised key, nothing spawns the executable, no timeout, no preemption of the other managed sources) filed off two pages; f108 is the other half of the same sentence - the source SET is short by the tamper-resistant OS policy channel and the convenience tier. One plan, because the composition rule they all depend on is single: sources do not merge, and a configured `policyHelper` preempts every other managed source.
units.rationale: An enterprise deployment can ship policy through the OS-managed channel it already uses for other apps, and can point at a helper executable instead of a static file. Crosses a persistence boundary (a new managed source file per platform) and a wire boundary (delivered policy resolution and `storage-runtime` bootstrap order), and it spawns a subprocess during bootstrap, so process lifecycle and timeout behaviour are risk triggers the plan must prove once on the final diff.

units.name: sandbox-path-settings
units.title: Sandbox filesystem key names, nesting, and path-prefix expansion
units.why: Both sit on the same parse boundary in `sandbox-settings.ts` plus its managed floor in `managed-policy.ts`, and they are complementary halves: f022 is the key spelling and nesting (`filesystem.allowWrite` versus `additionalWritableRoots`, one level up), whose enforcement half is already correct; f023 is the prefix grammar those keys' values may use (`~/`, `./`, and bare entries all throw instead of resolving). Fixing the key names without the prefix expansion leaves the documented examples still failing.
units.rationale: A user or admin can copy Claude's documented sandbox block verbatim, including `~/`-relative paths, and get the writable and denied roots they asked for instead of a parse throw. Crosses a persistence boundary (`SandboxSettingsV1` is the on-disk shape of `config.json`'s sandbox block) and a delivered-policy wire boundary, so the merge and floor composition must keep old files parsing.

units.name: model-selection-defaults
units.title: Fallback-model chain arity and per-model default effort
units.why: f226 and f242 are the same key filed off two pages: `fallbackModel` is typed `string` where the doc gives a list of up to three, and `storage.ts:273-276` silently coerces a doc-shaped array to the empty string, so writing the documented value disables the feature. f107 is the sibling defect one field away in the same files (`config-defaults.json`, `config/storage.ts`, `config-defaults-schema.ts`): effort defaults to `medium` for every model where the page requires `high`, with `xhigh` on Opus 4.7, and the model id is never an input to `resolveEffortLevel`. One plan because they share the defaults schema and the same silent-coercion failure mode.
units.rationale: A user configuring a fallback chain gets all three hops instead of a silently disabled feature, and every model runs at the effort level its own docs specify rather than a flat `medium`. Crosses a persistence boundary - the accepted type of a `config.json` key changes from scalar to list - so the plan must accept both shapes and state which one is written back.

units.name: statusline-surfaces
units.title: statusLine and subagentStatusLine: settings key, runner, and row override
units.why: Two absences of one mechanism at two scopes. Neither key is read at any scope, neither has a command runner, and both need the same pieces: the stdin payload shape, `COLUMNS`/`LINES` export, the refresh tick, and - for the subagent variant - the NDJSON id/content parser with hide-on-empty and keep-default-on-omitted-id. Building the main statusline without the subagent one would duplicate the runner.
units.rationale: A user gets the status row their `statusLine` command produces, and per-agent rows in the agent panel from `subagentStatusLine`, without editing source. Crosses a persistence boundary (two new `StoredConfig` keys plus their validators at user, project and managed scope) and spawns a user-supplied command on a timer, so process lifecycle and output-size handling are risk triggers.

units.name: hook-input-payload-parity
units.title: Documented fields missing or misnamed on hook stdin payloads
units.why: Six findings, one object: `SdkAutomationInput` and the `lifecycle-bridge.ts` emission that fills it. f002 (`file_path`), f003 (`new_cwd`/`old_cwd` aliases), f004 (an `error` projection instead of the raw Nessy `ErrorCode`), f007 (two absent PreCompact/PostCompact fields) and f009/f218 (the same missing `effort: { level }` object plus `$CLAUDE_EFFORT` on both env surfaces, filed off two pages) are all field-level deltas on payloads whose names, matchers and delivery already conform. They must be one plan because they edit the same type and the same emitter, and `git commit <pathspec>` takes working-tree state.
units.rationale: A hook script copied from Claude's docs reads the fields it expects - `file_path`, `new_cwd`, `error`, `effort.level` - instead of finding them absent or under a Nessy name. Crosses the subprocess-to-host IPC wire (the `automation_event` envelope) and the hook process boundary (stdin JSON plus `NESSY_EVENT_DATA` and `CLAUDE_*` env), and the payload type is frozen in `AGENT_EVENT_CONTRACTS_V1`, so the packaged Pi bundle must be rebuilt with the host.

units.name: hook-output-and-process-env
units.title: Hook output decision keys, the block-cap lever, and the hook env-file channel
units.why: All four live in `parseHookCommandOutput`, `hook-decision-contract.ts` and `buildHookCommandEnv` - what a hook may say back and what environment it runs in. f010 (four of five SessionStart output keys absent at parser, surface table and decision type) and f216 (`sessionTitle` on UserPromptSubmit) are the same missing-output-key shape; f012 is the absent `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP` lever over the Stop-decision streak the same parser feeds; f141 is the `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` channel in both directions, and its writer is the same `buildHookCommandEnv` the effort work touches.
units.rationale: A hook can set the session title, use the documented SessionStart output keys, raise or disable the block cap, and export variables into subsequent Bash commands through a per-session env file. Crosses the hook process and trust boundary in both directions - we now read a file a hook wrote and inject it into the shell environment - which makes trust and path containment the plan's central risk, plus a persistence boundary for the session title.

units.name: memory-load-limits
units.title: The 25KB memory cap, and moving the 200-line cap onto the live route
units.why: Four findings off four pages describing one pair of deltas: the 25KB byte limit has no representation anywhere in the repo, and `MEMORY_LOAD_LINE_LIMIT = 200` exists with the right value but lives in `readMemoryFile`, which on a shipped build serves only the legacy composer and the import scan - the pinned route every turn actually takes (`composePinnedCapabilityContext` into `materializer.readText`, and the Pi twin) reads `MEMORY.md` whole. One implementation closes all four, and it must land before anything else changes what those limits count.
units.rationale: A large `MEMORY.md` stops silently consuming the whole context window on every turn: it is truncated at 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first, on the route the model actually reads. No persistence or wire change - the caps are read-time - but the pinned-capability path is shared by both shipping backends, so the plan needs a positive control proving truncation happens on a packaged build and not only in the legacy composer.

units.name: memory-import-recognition
units.title: @path import recognition: position, file family, Markdown awareness, comment stripping
units.why: One recogniser, three layers of the same rule. f099 is where a token may appear (we require first non-whitespace; the page allows anywhere in the line, several per line) and which files expand at all; f100 is the Markdown-awareness pass that must run inside the same scan, since fenced blocks are followed today; f101 is HTML-comment stripping plus the fact that comment and frontmatter lines are counted by the line cap instead of stripped before measurement. Splitting them would mean rewriting the same scanner three times.
units.rationale: The import examples in Claude's own memory page work: imports are found mid-line and in `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`, paths inside fenced code blocks are left alone, and maintainer HTML comments stop reaching the model. Crosses a persistence-adjacent boundary in that the set of files pulled into context changes, and it reads new paths off disk, so the plan must state the containment rule for a newly-followed import.

units.name: memory-write-feedback
units.title: Post-write memory measurement, over-limit error, and frontmatter timestamp
units.why: f103 and f166 are the same absent synchronous feedback loop filed off two pages: nothing measures `MEMORY.md` after a write, so neither the near-limit reminder nor the hard over-limit error exists, and both writers return unconditional success. f102 is the other thing the same writer must do - inspect the first line for a frontmatter fence and maintain a `modified` key - and it shares the measurement exclusion, since frontmatter is not counted.
units.rationale: When the model or the user saves a memory that pushes the index over the limit, they are told at write time instead of silently losing the tail at load time, and a memory file with frontmatter keeps an accurate `modified` timestamp. Crosses a persistence boundary: both writers change what they write to `MEMORY.md`, and the tool result the model receives changes from unconditional success to a possible error, which is a contract the session tool's schema advertises.

units.name: memory-discovery-scopes
units.title: Two missing instruction-file scopes: the cwd .claude/CLAUDE.md and the system tier
units.why: Both are one absent candidate in the same eager discovery list in `native-sources.ts`, with nothing wrong about the existing behaviour. f068 adds `join(workingDirectory, '.claude', 'CLAUDE.md')`; f207 adds the highest-authority, un-excludable system tier, whose per-platform directory is already resolved for `managed-policy.json` and whose `builtin` scope kind already ranks 0 in `scopeSpecificity`. Same file, same ordering rule, complementary ends of the scope chain.
units.rationale: A repo that keeps its instructions at `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is picked up without moving the file, and an administrator can ship organisation-wide instructions that a project cannot exclude. Crosses a persistence boundary in the sense that a new on-disk location becomes load-bearing, and the system tier is admin-authored, so the plan must prove the exclusion mechanism cannot reach it.

units.name: mcp-server-config-and-connect
units.title: What an MCP server config may say, and the environment and headers we connect with
units.why: Five findings on one boundary: the parse of an MCP server entry and the connect that follows it. f037 and f041 are the same missing `streamable-http` spelling filed off two pages, absent from four closed transport sets and from the plugin schema; f042 is the `headersHelper` command whose value we parse and never execute; f044 is the absent `MCP_TIMEOUT` lever over a `connectTimeoutMs` whose value is already correct; f221 is the project-dir spawn variable, narrower than documented for native and `.mcp.json` stdio servers and emitted under the wrong key for plugin ones. They share `project-config.ts`, `server-config-values.ts`, `mcp-pool.ts` and the two format adapters.
units.rationale: A server entry copied verbatim from an MCP server's own README connects - including the `streamable-http` type, a `headersHelper` for rotating credentials, `MCP_TIMEOUT` for a slow server, and `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` in a stdio command. Crosses a persistence boundary (plugin normalization runs at install time and writes the normalized config) and a wire boundary (headers and env now reach a third-party process at connect), and `headersHelper` spawns a command whose stdout becomes an auth header - a credential path the plan must scope explicitly.

units.name: mcp-roots-and-channels
units.title: MCP roots capability and the channel notification envelope
units.why: Four findings on the MCP protocol surfaces beyond tools, all in `mcp/client.ts` and `mcp-pool.ts`. f040 is the entire client-side roots surface (capability declaration with `listChanged`, the `roots/list` handler, the change notification); f135 is two wrong ingress strings including the method literal `claude/channel` where the contract says `notifications/claude/channel`; f136 is the missing envelope, since `meta` is never parsed around a channel body that is otherwise right; f134 is the delivery semantics of the same channels, where idle arrival is unsupported because we require a turn in flight. Splitting them would mean touching the same client twice.
units.rationale: A third-party MCP server can ask which directories the session covers and can push channel updates that arrive while the session is idle, under the method name the contract specifies. Crosses a wire boundary directly: the `capabilities` object in the MCP `initialize` handshake changes for every server we connect to, and a new request method becomes callable from a third party into our process, so the handler's authorization and the data it may reveal are the plan's central risk.

units.name: tool-result-size-thresholds
units.title: The tool-result persist threshold and its MCP-specific settings
units.why: A single self-contained contract with a wide blast radius: `guardLargeResult` has twelve call sites, and the MCP persist threshold is 12,000 estimated tokens where the documented value is 25,000, so every result in the 12k-25k band is replaced by a file reference where Claude hands it to the model. Kept out of the MCP config plan because it is about result size across all tool paths, not about connecting.
units.rationale: Mid-sized MCP and tool results - roughly 48KB to 100KB of text - reach the model directly instead of being spilled to a file the model then has to open, matching Claude's behaviour on the same payload. No persistence change, but it alters what crosses the model boundary on twelve call sites, so the plan should prove the threshold once per distinct call-site class rather than per site.

units.name: headless-init-frame
units.title: The headless system/init frame and its CI-gating arrays
units.why: Three findings off three pages describing one absent object: the mandated first stream object does not exist, so `plugins`, `plugin_errors`, `mcp_servers`, `mcp_server_errors` and the optional `capabilities` array have nowhere to live, and `mcp_server_errors` additionally has no producer wired to it. One plan, one file (`apps/cli/src/index.ts`) plus the capabilities views that feed it.
units.rationale: A CI job can gate on the first line of `nessy-general-agent -p` output - failing the build when a plugin or MCP server failed to load - instead of having no machine-readable signal at all. Crosses a wire boundary: it adds a new frame to the headless NDJSON stream that external consumers parse, so the plan must fix the frame's schema and say what a consumer that ignores unknown objects sees. It also needs an error-collection producer for MCP config failures, which is why it follows the MCP config plan.

units.name: headless-cli-flags-and-exit
units.title: Headless flag names, exit codes, output cap, and session-retention default
units.why: Four findings on the same file and the same process contract. f179 is `--permission-mode` spelled `--mode` plus two non-cosmetic deltas; f176 is SIGTERM exiting 130 instead of 143 through a shared handler with a constant code; f178 is the entirely absent output byte cap, which must count the init frame the previous plan adds; f126 is the inverted session-retention default, where the same command keeps a resumable session upstream and hard-deletes it here. A supervisor script cares about all four together.
units.rationale: A CI or supervisor script can pass Claude's documented flags, distinguish an operator Ctrl-C from an infrastructure SIGTERM, rely on a bounded stream, and keep its session resumable by default. Crosses a persistence boundary - the retention default decides whether a session record survives the run - and a process and wire boundary in the exit-code contract, so the plan must state the migration for scripts relying on the current `--mode` spelling.

units.name: hook-firing-and-await
units.title: When lifecycle hooks fire, what trigger they carry, and whether the host waits
units.why: Four findings about occurrence rather than payload. f001 inverts Setup's firing rule (we fire on every Pi `session_start`; the doc excludes exactly that case) and needs a launch mode that does not exist to derive `init`/`maintenance` from. f005 is the same shape: ConfigChanged fires on runtime session-config commits, a set disjoint from the documented settings, managed-policy and skill-file changes. f006 over-fires on every plain turn where the doc fires on command expansion. f217 is the missing awaited round trip on PreCompact, that is, whether the verdict is read at all. All four change what crosses the subprocess-to-host wire and what a stored matcher means.
units.rationale: An imported Claude Setup hook stops running an npm-install-class command on every new chat, a correctly-matched `init`/`maintenance` hook becomes runnable, ConfigChanged fires on the file changes it documents, and a PreCompact hook's decision is actually honoured. Crosses two wire boundaries and one persistence boundary: it adds a launch-mode field to the session-create RPC, changes what the Pi subprocess emits, and - most importantly - changes the MEANING of already-saved `automations.json` records, since a stored catch-all Setup automation stops running every session. That behaviour-change-without-schema-change is the plan's headline risk. It follows the headless plan because the new launch mode lands in the same CLI file.

units.name: subagent-nesting-depth
units.title: Subagent nesting depth: default 3 and its override
units.why: Four findings off four pages, one knob: the nesting budget defaults to 1 where every page says 3, and depth 1 is precisely Claude's documented nesting-off setting, so we ship an opt-out as unconditional product behaviour - plus there is no override to raise it. One plan, and it leads the orchestration family because every other orchestration plan's fixtures and semaphore arithmetic are written against the current depth.
units.rationale: A subagent can spawn a subagent, so multi-layer workflows and review chains that work in Claude Code work here, and an operator can raise or lower the ceiling. Crosses a wire boundary (the harness manifest carries the depth to the Pi subprocess) and a persistence boundary (a new settings key for the override), and it changes concurrency behaviour under load, which is why it must land before the concurrency plan.

units.name: subagent-limits-and-child-output
units.title: Subagent concurrency ceilings, output cap with disk spill, and instruction-shaped output marking
units.why: Three findings that all edit `orchestrator/subagent-tool.ts` and its siblings, and all concern what the orchestrator enforces on a child run and what it hands back. f086 is one semaphore serving two documented independent ceilings, with the workflow number applied to subagents and the wrong failure mode; f165 is the output cap - no disk spill, an untunable constant, and a `get_subagent_result` fallback that returns less than the parent already had; f090 is the absent marker line for a child report whose text matches permission-setting patterns. File overlap makes them one plan by the repo's own zoning rule.
units.rationale: Parallel subagents run up to the documented ceiling instead of six on an eight-core machine, a truncated child report names a file holding the full output, the cap is tunable, and a child report that talks about `bypassPermissions` arrives annotated rather than bare. Crosses a wire boundary (the child-session port carries the spill path) and a trust boundary - the marker line is a prompt-injection guard on text the parent model reads - so the plan needs a positive control proving the marker appears, not just that the pattern exists.

units.name: agent-memory-directories
units.title: Per-agent memory directories and the prompt block that names them
units.why: The same absent filesystem half filed off two pages: the frontmatter key, its three scope words and its validation all match the page, and none of the three directories (`agent-memory/<name>/`, `agent-memory-local/<name>/`, `<configDir>/agent-memory/<name>/`) is ever derived or created, `composeChildPrompt` emits no block naming one, and no `MEMORY.md` is read from it. One mechanism, one plan.
units.rationale: A subagent accumulates its own notes across runs and reads them back, which is the entire point of the agent-memory key authors are already allowed to write. Crosses a persistence boundary - new directories are auto-created and written to under the project and the config dir - so path derivation, containment and the local-versus-committed scope split are the plan's risk, and it follows the memory plans because it reads through the same `memory-store.ts`.

units.name: agent-definition-fields
units.title: Agent definition fields: initialPrompt and name normalization
units.why: Both are the agent-definition frontmatter contract in `shared/agents/definitions.ts` and its Pi wire descriptor. f211 is `initialPrompt`, absent from the definition type, both frontmatter readers, the wire descriptor and both strict validators, and discarded without a diagnostic - plus the scope the doc gives it has no runner. f220 is the other half of the name-matching rule: case and trim folding are implemented, separator folding is not, so a hyphen, underscore or space variant is rejected in both directions.
units.rationale: An agent author's `initialPrompt` line is honoured instead of silently dropped, and an agent is reachable by its kebab, snake or spaced spelling. Crosses a wire boundary (the Pi runtime agent descriptor gains a field) and a persistence boundary (agent definition files and the config defaults schema), and a name-matching widening can newly collide two agents, so the plan must state the collision verdict.

units.name: workflow-invocation-contract
units.title: Workflow invocation: undefined args and the child permission floor
units.why: Both are what a workflow run hands its script and its children. f095 is the substitution when `args` is not supplied - Claude leaves the global undefined, we hand an empty object and on the slash path an object with an empty `input`, so every documented no-input branch is dead. f094 is the missing `acceptEdits` floor for workflow-spawned children, which today take the ordinary subagent inheritance path; the child is not even labelled as belonging to a workflow at the spawn site, which is the same labelling gap f095's slash path exposes.
units.rationale: A workflow script's no-input branch runs when the workflow is invoked without arguments, and a workflow's children can edit files without a per-edit prompt as documented. Crosses a wire boundary (the workflow tool's argument object and the child spawn descriptor gain a workflow label) and a permission boundary - raising a child's effective mode is a permission decision, an explicit risk trigger - so the floor must be proven to be a floor and not a raise past the parent.

units.name: skill-visibility-settings
units.title: The skill visibility settings key and its four states
units.why: One absent settings-side mechanism filed off two pages: no key of any spelling reaches skill visibility, so the four states, the absent-means-on default and the `.claude/settings.local.json` destination have no implementation, and two of the four states are not expressible even by hand-editing the SKILL.md. It leads the skills family because `disable-model-invocation` and `user-invocable` semantics settle here, and the command and code-review plans both consume them.
units.rationale: A user can hide a skill from the model, or make it user-invocable only, from settings - without editing a file they may not own. Crosses a persistence boundary (a new key in a Claude settings file we do not currently read) and changes what reaches the model's system prompt, so the plan must state precedence against the SKILL.md frontmatter that expresses the nearest two states today.

units.name: skill-frontmatter-runtime
units.title: Skill bash placeholders and the context/agent/hooks frontmatter consumers
units.why: Both are the SKILL.md contract at runtime, in `runtime-skill-content.ts` and its context twin. f058 is the placeholder grammar and insertion point - a bare column-0 bang where the doc has an inline backtick form anywhere, exactly one where the doc allows unlimited - with the execution machinery around it already correct. f062 is the frontmatter fields whose names and values match the page exactly and have no consumer: `context: fork` runs inline with full history, `background` is inert, `agent` is repurposed. Same file, same materialization pass.
units.rationale: A skill copied from Claude's docs works: its inline command placeholders expand wherever they appear, and a `context: fork` skill runs isolated in a subagent whose prompt is the SKILL.md instead of polluting the main conversation. Crosses the command-execution boundary (more command sites per skill, and the permission gate must hold for each) and the session wire for a forked result arriving as a separate completion.

units.name: skill-discovery-precedence
units.title: Descendant skill discovery and the global-over-project alias rule
units.why: Both decide which skill a bare name resolves to. f063 is the absent descendant half of discovery - no code path reads a skills directory below the working directory, and there is no first-touch lazy load to compensate. f170 is the one ordering term that makes global outrank project for kind `skill` in `scopeSpecificity`, which today has project above global. Discovery and precedence must be one plan because widening discovery changes which pairs collide.
units.rationale: In a monorepo, a skill defined under `apps/web/.agents/skills/` is available in a session opened at the repo root, and a user's own skill wins the unqualified name over a project one, as documented. Crosses a persistence-adjacent boundary in that the inventoried skill set grows from a filesystem walk, so the plan must bound the walk and say what happens on a large tree - and the precedence flip must be scoped to kind `skill`, not applied to `scopeSpecificity` globally.

units.name: custom-command-expansion
units.title: Custom slash commands: skill precedence, positional arguments, and multi-skill runs
units.why: Three findings on the same command parse and expansion path. f144 is the inverted precedence between a skill and a command of the same name, where the loser is dropped instead of kept under its namespaced id; f145 is the entirely unimplemented positional family (`$0`, `$1`, `$ARGUMENTS[N]`, and escaping), whose correct implementation already exists 200 lines away as a module-private helper in `runtime-skill-content.ts`; f149 is the leading run of up to six skills with the same trailing text given to each, unrepresentable end to end while `customSlashCommandId` is singular. Same parse, same expander.
units.rationale: A command body using `$1` gets the first argument instead of the literal text, typing several skill commands in a row runs all of them, and a name collision keeps both entries addressable. Crosses a wire boundary - `customSlashCommandId` changes from a scalar to a list on the session RPC - so the plan must keep an older client's scalar accepted.

units.name: code-review-contract
units.title: The code-review entry point, target grammar, and the outcome field
units.why: Two layers of one feature. f143 is the review command itself: model-invocable only where the doc is the exact inverse, uncommitted-only scope where the doc is upstream-relative, a narrower target grammar with no path, PR number or ref range, and no fix or comment modes. f142 is the field the same feature's results need - `outcome` is absent from `FindingSchema`, and because the projected schema sets `additionalProperties: false` we actively advertise that it cannot exist, so the documented re-report-after-fixes flow has no representation. Fixing one without the other leaves the feature half-usable.
units.rationale: A user can run a review from the command surface over the diff Claude reviews by default (branch commits ahead of upstream plus uncommitted), target a path, PR or ref range, and see per-finding outcomes after fixes are applied. Crosses a wire boundary: the ReportFindings tool schema is advertised to the model with `additionalProperties: false`, so widening it changes a published tool contract and the harness tool-surface fixture.

units.name: builtin-session-commands
units.title: Built-in session commands: /clear, /btw, /recap
units.why: All three extend the same three structures - the built-in command id union, `parseSessionCommand`, and the `SessionCommand` wire union - and today all three strings reach the model as ordinary prose. f124 and f183 are the same `/btw` mechanism filed off two pages (plus `/recap`), needing a non-persisting answer channel whose two ingredients (a tool-less `queryLlm` call and the in-memory transcript) exist unconnected. f074 is `/clear`, which no code path claims and no backend has an arm for. One parser, one wire union, one plan.
units.rationale: Typing `/clear` resets the conversation instead of being sent to the model as text, and `/btw` answers a side question without adding a turn to the transcript. Crosses a persistence boundary (`/clear` truncates or forks the stored session) and a wire boundary (three new members on the `SessionCommand` union, which an older client must tolerate), and the `/btw` channel must be provably excluded from history - an absence claim that needs a positive control.

units.name: shell-command-response-mode
units.title: The shell-command response mode and its default
units.why: A single self-contained contract: the shell mode's response half does not exist - no code path dispatches a turn on the shell transcript - so the documented default `respondToBashCommands: true` has nothing to switch on. Kept separate from the built-in commands plan because it is an input-mode behaviour with its own settings key and its own dispatch path.
units.rationale: Running a shell command from the composer gets the model's comment on the output, as documented, and the setting that disables it does something. Crosses a persistence boundary (a new `StoredConfig` key with a non-false default) and a wire boundary (the shell-command payload in `protocol/dto.ts`), and it dispatches a model turn on command output the user did not explicitly send, so the plan must state the opt-out clearly.

units.name: worktree-lifecycle
units.title: Worktree creation include-list, default-branch freshness, and post-removal cleanup
units.why: Five findings, all in `server-core/src/pi-harness/worktree-*.ts`, covering one lifecycle. f096, f147 and f159 are the identical absent `.worktreeinclude` mechanism filed off three pages - nothing opens the file, nothing parses gitignore syntax for it, nothing copies a file into a worktree. f097 is the freshness prelude before the `origin/HEAD` read, whose own value and fallbacks are already correct. f186 is the missing local git-config cleanup after removal. Create, resolve, remove: one plan.
units.rationale: A worktree session starts with the untracked files the project declares it needs (`.env`, local configs) instead of a broken build, branches off a fresh default branch, and leaves no stale local git config behind. Crosses a wire boundary in that the worktree plan is computed server-side and executed as git commands, and it copies files into a new tree, so path containment and the never-copy set are the plan's risk.

units.name: scheduled-task-catchup
units.title: Missed scheduled runs and per-task worktree isolation
units.why: Both are the scheduled-task record and its runner in `shared/automations/`. f161 is the entire absent missed-run mechanism: no persisted per-task last-occurrence cursor, no start-time sweep, no seven-day window, and - the detail that shapes the fix - a replayed SchedulerTick matches nothing because `matchesBasePredicate` evaluates the cron against the current minute. f162 is the absent per-task worktree toggle on the same persisted matcher, plus the missing call after `createSession`. Same schema, same write surfaces, same hand-off.
units.rationale: A scheduled task that was due while the app was closed runs on next start instead of being lost, and a task can run in its own worktree so it does not disturb the working tree. Crosses a persistence boundary twice - a new per-task cursor and a new boolean on `AutomationMatcherSchema`, which must survive both write surfaces and the PendingPrompt hand-off that copies a fixed field list - so schema forward-compatibility is the plan's central risk.

units.name: loop-and-self-paced-scheduling
units.title: The /loop surface, its default prompt, and self-paced wakeups
units.why: Three layers of one feature over `shared/sessions/cron-*` and `session-cron-service`. f199 is the entry point: no bundled skill, no interval grammar, no self-paced mode, with everything below it already at parity. f200 is the default prompt resolution (a `loop.md` at either scope, plus the built-in maintenance prompt it falls back to) that a bare `/loop` needs. f201 is the self-paced half: no ScheduleWakeup tool at any layer, and `SessionCronRecord` can only express a cron string, so even a correctly-named tool would have nothing to write.
units.rationale: A user can run a prompt on an interval with `/loop 5m`, get the documented maintenance prompt by default, override it with a `loop.md`, and let the model pace itself by scheduling its own next wakeup. Crosses a persistence boundary: `SessionCronRecord` must represent a delay as well as a cron expression, so the store's schema changes and older records must keep loading. It also adds a model-callable tool that schedules future work, which is a lifecycle risk trigger.

units.name: marketplace-auto-update
units.title: Per-marketplace autoUpdate and the managed pin
units.why: Three findings on the `marketplaces.json` registry row and the managed policy that delivers it. f025 and f046 are the same absent `autoUpdate` mechanism off two pages - unparsed from managed policy, unpersisted on the row, unexposed on the wire, absent from the UI, with a polarity-dependent default; f047 is the sibling managed key for pinning and annotating a marketplace on the Discover tab, actively rejected as unknown today. Same row, same managed schema, same RPC and the same PluginsPage surface.
units.rationale: An organisation can pin a marketplace and control whether its plugins update themselves, and a user sees which marketplaces are managed. Crosses a persistence boundary (a new field on the `marketplaces.json` row, which older builds must tolerate) and a wire boundary (`SafeMarketplaceCatalogItem` and the marketplace RPC both gain fields), and auto-update fetches and installs code without a user step, so the plan must state the trust gate.

units.name: plugin-install-and-dependencies
units.title: Dependency acquisition and session-scoped installs
units.why: Both are the install path in `plugins/install-service.ts` and `management-service-v2.ts`. f048 is the acquisition half of plugin dependencies: the manifest key, the descriptor shapes and every load-time rule are already correct, and nothing ever fetches a missing dependency. f244 is session scope - `PluginScope` has three persistent members and the capability assembly accepts only committed entries, so the nearest shipped behaviour writes an installed record, the exact opposite of the documented one. Both change what an install writes, in the same file.
units.rationale: Installing a plugin brings its declared dependencies with it instead of failing at load, and a plugin can be tried for one session without leaving an installed record behind. Crosses a persistence boundary directly - `PluginScope` gains a non-persistent member and the installed-entry writer must learn not to write - so the plan must prove the absence of a record with a positive control, and dependency acquisition fetches code, which is a supply-chain trust decision to state explicitly.

units.name: plugin-bundle-component-shapes
units.title: Doc-conformant plugin bundle layouts and plugin-provided settings
units.why: Both are what a plugin bundle may contain that we currently ignore. f054 is discovery: no scanner stats a nested `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` under the skills dir, and `skillRecords` gates on `SKILL.md` alone, so a doc-conformant bundle contributes nothing and the subset that happens to carry a root `SKILL.md` degrades to a bare skill with its agents, hooks and MCP silently dropped. f053 is the bundle's own `settings.json`, which nothing parses, so neither documented key is read. Same scanner, same capability assembly.
units.rationale: A plugin authored exactly as Claude's reference describes installs with all its components - agents, hooks, MCP servers, skills - instead of silently contributing a fraction of itself, and a bundle's own settings, including its subagent status line, take effect. Crosses a persistence boundary (the capability inventory and the installed entry shape both grow) and it makes plugin-authored settings load-bearing, so precedence against user settings is the plan's central decision.

units.name: egress-and-provider-routing
units.title: Proxy bypass parsing, provider routing env lists, and gateway request hardening
units.why: Four findings on how a credential-carrying outbound request is routed and bounded. f116 and f118 are literally the same two hand-copied lists in `options.ts:260-262` and `llm-connections.ts:931-935`, short by three Mantle names and by `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` and `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY` - the duplication is why they drifted, so deduplication is the fix for both. f191 is the absent `redirect: 'error'` and 3-second timeout at two fetch call sites, where a 30x today forwards the gateway JWT to a third host. f093 is the missing whitespace separator in `NO_PROXY`, which silently degrades a documented spelling to one unmatchable rule. All four decide where a secret may go.
units.rationale: A gateway or provider request stops following a redirect that would hand its JWT to another host, the documented Bedrock and Vertex/Foundry routing variables are recognised and correctly tiered, and a whitespace-separated `NO_PROXY` bypasses what it says. Crosses a wire boundary and an auth boundary - these are the lists that decide which credentials go to which endpoint - which makes it a risk trigger; the leak fix should land early and be provable with a redirecting test endpoint.

units.name: permission-tool-classification
units.title: Tool identity and state-change classification in the permission path
units.why: Both are what string or class a permission decision keys off. f021 is one binding whose value is right and name is ours: `stopTask` where the documented name is `TaskStop`, on the two axes that matter (permission rules and hook matchers). f139 is the absent classification step: read-only and state-changing browser verbs collapse onto one verdict, so all 32 verbs behave alike in `plan` mode. Same decision point, and both change what a saved rule matches.
units.rationale: A permission rule or hook matcher written against Claude's documented tool name works, and in plan mode a browser navigation or click is gated while a read is not. Crosses a persistence boundary (saved permission rules reference the old tool name and need an alias or migration) and a wire boundary (the harness tool descriptor and its contract fixture), and it is a permission decision - an explicit risk trigger - so both the old and new spellings must be proven on the final diff.

units.name: project-trust-home-carveout
units.title: The home directory must not receive a persisted trust grant
units.why: A single one-branch carve-out with a security consequence. The session-only mechanism exists and works - a process-only persistence keeps a decision in `ProjectTrustStore.processOnly`, salted with a per-process random value so it expires with the process - and the home directory never reaches it, because persistence is decided solely by stat success, so `$HOME` classifies as stable and its grant is persisted.
units.rationale: Trusting a session opened at the home directory stops permanently trusting everything under it; the grant lapses with the process, as documented. Crosses a persistence boundary - it changes what `ProjectTrustStore` writes, and existing persisted home grants must be handled rather than silently honoured - and it is a trust decision, so the plan must prove the negative (nothing on disk after the process ends) with a positive control.

units.name: deep-link-safety
units.title: Deep links must not execute actions without a user step
units.why: One page, one half of it, and it is the security half: an OS- or web-delivered link is not inert - a send flag reaches `sendMessage` with no user step, and six further cases in the same switch mutate state (delete-session, delete-source, rename, flag, set-mode, oauth), where the documented handler accepts one path, open. The directory half already complies, so the plan is a narrowing of one switch plus a confirmation surface.
units.rationale: A link from a web page or another app can open the target but cannot send a message, delete a session or change permission mode on the user's behalf without an explicit confirmation. Crosses a trust boundary from outside the process into state-mutating RPCs - the strongest risk trigger in this set - so the plan must enumerate the switch exhaustively and prove each removed case, and it needs new i18n strings for the confirmation surface.

units.name: output-styles
units.title: Output style placement, the two missing built-ins, and the project directory chain
units.why: Three findings on `prompts/output-styles.ts` and the two composers that read it, with the mechanism itself fully built. f193 is the second documented placement - the style text reaches the model once, in the system prefix, and not per request. f194 is set composition: Proactive and Learning are simply absent from `BUILTIN_OUTPUT_STYLE_DEFINITIONS`. f195 is the project-directory SET, one level deep instead of the whole chain, with the precedence rule and per-directory read already correct. Same file, three complementary deltas.
units.rationale: A chosen output style actually holds through a long turn rather than fading after the system prefix, the two missing built-in styles are selectable, and a style defined higher in the repo applies in a nested directory. No persistence change; it changes what crosses the model boundary on every request on both backends, so the plan should measure prompt composition once per backend rather than per style.

units.name: claude-informational-messages
units.title: The informational system subtype dropped by the Claude event adapter
units.why: A single unhandled branch with a defined blast radius: `adaptSystem` has no arm for the informational subtype and no trailing else, so `content`, `level`, `tool_use_id` and `prevent_continuation` are discarded outright. Self-contained in `agent/backend/claude/event-adapter.ts` plus the message type and the frozen adjacent-backend fixture.
units.rationale: On the Claude backend, informational system messages reach the user - including the ones that carry `prevent_continuation`, which today is dropped along with the rest. Crosses a wire boundary: `packages/core/src/types/message.ts` and `protocol/dto.ts` gain a frame, and the adjacent-backend frozen-contract fixture pins the existing set, so the plan must update that fixture deliberately rather than as a side effect.

units.name: keybindings-config
units.title: The keybindings.json loader, action-id vocabulary, and contexts
units.why: One absent mechanism in four separable pieces that only make sense together: nothing reads a `keybindings.json`, so the declared `userOverrides` map is permanently empty and no user can rebind anything by any route; the action-id vocabulary uses a dot where the page uses a colon; the nineteen file-level context names have no counterpart; and live reload has none either. There is no smaller coherent slice.
units.rationale: A user can rebind a shortcut by editing a config file and see it take effect without restarting. Crosses a persistence boundary (a new user-scoped config file with its own schema and loader) and a wire boundary (the settings RPC and the renderer action registry must agree on the id spelling), and the id rename touches every registered action, so the plan must decide whether the dotted spelling stays accepted.

units.name: goal-completion-state
units.title: Goal completion must clear the goal and record an achieved entry
units.why: The smallest self-contained unit in the set and the most surgical: on a complete verdict we write `complete_suggested` and keep the record active, and even if that were flipped, `validTerminalState` would reject the record on reload because it demands a manual evaluation source. Two edits in one file, and the correct enum values already exist in every schema.
units.rationale: When the evaluator judges a goal met, the goal clears and an achieved entry is recorded instead of the goal staying active with a suggestion attached forever. Crosses a persistence boundary - the goal record's terminal state changes and the reload validator must accept the new source - so already-stored `complete_suggested` records need a stated migration.

units.name: web-search-budget
units.title: The per-session web-search budget and its over-cap notice
units.why: One absent mechanism with three named pieces in one tool: no per-session count of web_search calls, no 200 default and no env lever, and no over-cap result - and the shape of the third piece is load-bearing, because the existing failure path returns an error flag and the documented over-cap behaviour must not, being a non-error notice telling the model to continue with what it has.
units.rationale: A session that loops on web search stops burning quota indefinitely: after the budget the model is told to continue with what it has instead of receiving an error. Crosses the subprocess boundary - the count lives with the tool in the Pi subprocess while the budget is host configuration, so it travels the child-session port - and it changes a tool result shape the model reads, which the plan must distinguish from the error path.

units.name: host-diagnostics-rpc
units.title: Host diagnostics: the git-bash filename predicate and /heapdump
units.why: Both are host-environment diagnostics delivered over the system and status RPC surface, and both are a shape mismatch rather than a missing idea. f208 accepts only `bash.exe` where the page specifies `bash.exe`, `sh.exe`, `bash` and `sh`, with two second-order deltas riding on the same predicate (the Browse dialog's exe-only filter, and a hard user-facing failure instead of a soft one). f210 is `/heapdump`: the only memory data we produce is `ServerStatus.memory`, three counters delivered over RPC to a caller that never displays them, where the doc requires four buckets persisted to a file.
units.rationale: A Windows user whose Git ships `sh.exe` gets a working shell instead of a hard rejection, and anyone diagnosing a memory problem can produce the documented heap breakdown on disk. Crosses a wire boundary (`ServerStatus` and the system RPC both change shape) and writes a diagnostics file to a user directory, so the output path and what the dump may contain are the plan's disclosure risk.
